title: Cover
text: φ Antocci Physics Day 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools Acceleration: When Velocity Changes Our constant-velocity model was an approximation. How good was it? Fictional scenario · illustration not to scale · the physics is real

title: How this lesson works
text: Before you start · your group ≈ 2 min How this lesson works Slideshow lead Reads each slide aloud and moves the deck forward. Whiteboard scribe Holds the dry erase marker and works problems at the whiteboard. Timekeeper · support Starts each timer and keeps the group on pace. Checker · support Asks "How do we know?" before anyone presses Show answer. Explicit instruction Read it together. Then one person restates it in their own words. Check your understanding Solve alone, compare answers, agree — then press Show answer. Group tasks Start the timer. Everyone contributes before you move on. Exit ticket On your own. Submit it with this lesson's assignment. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 02 / 30 2 students: lead + timekeeper, scribe + checker. 3 students: third person takes both support duties. Roles rotate at each discussion. Everyone submits their own work.

title: The asteroid thread
text: The asteroid thread What we know so far We've treated 2026-XJ's velocity as constant. That's an approximation — gravity is going to change it. Today Acceleration describes velocity changes. It explains why orbits work, and it becomes essential in Unit 2. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 04 / 30

title: Watch the gaps grow
text: See it → describe it Target R4 Watch the gaps grow Dots show equal time intervals. Bigger gaps mean greater speed. Moving farther each second The object is speeding up to the right. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 06 / 30

title: A velocity graph tells the change
text: See it → describe it Target R4 A velocity graph tells the change Velocity increases from 0 to 2 to 4 to 6 m/s. It gains 2 m/s each second. Velocity over time Acceleration is the rate of velocity change. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 07 / 30

title: A rate of change of a rate
text: Check your understanding Target R4 A rate of change of a rate A cart’s velocity changes from +2 to +8 m/s in 3 s. How much does its velocity change each second, on average? title: Acceleration
text: Definition ≈ 10 min Acceleration Acceleration a = Δv ÷ Δt Units m/s² Read it as "m/s, every second" Each second, your velocity changes by a m/s. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 09 / 30

title: What changes each second?
text: 2026-XJ · What Changes · Graphic novel, page 25 What changes each second? Nadia and Mei describe acceleration as how much velocity changes each second and in which direction. Their notebook shows acceleration equals change in velocity divided by elapsed time. Acceleration describes a change in velocity. Its units are meters per second, per second. How does a velocity change differ from a velocity? Explain with your own example. Part 1 · Compare velocity changes · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 7

title: Compare to gravity
text: The car, in physics units ≈ 10 min Compare to gravity 60 mph ≈ 27 m/s Car a ≈ 27 ÷ 6 ≈ 4.5 m/s² Free fall g ≈ 9.8 m/s² The car has roughly half of g. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 11 / 30

title: Slowing down is accelerating, too.
text: Acceleration is a vector ≈ 10 min Slowing down is accelerating, too. Slowing down means acceleration points opposite the motion — negative, if motion is positive. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 12 / 30

title: One step at a time
text: I do · find the change Target R4 One step at a time Velocity changes from 2 to 6 m/s in 2 s. Change: 6 − 2 = 4 m/s Velocity over time First compare the two velocities. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 13 / 30

title: Share the change across time
text: I do · find the rate Target R4 Share the change across time 4 m/s ÷ 2 s = 2 m/s² Say it: “velocity gains 2 m/s each second.” The velocity increase The bars show changes in velocity, not positions. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 14 / 30

title: Acceleration measures velocity change
text: Explicit instruction Target R4 Acceleration measures velocity change ā = (v f − v i ) / Δt Velocity can change in magnitude, direction, or both. Speeding up, slowing down, and turning can all involve acceleration. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 15 / 30

title: Speeding up, slowing down, or constant?
text: v–t graph practice ≈ 20 min Speeding up, slowing down, or constant? Slope up Speeding up (in +) Flat Constant velocity Slope down Slowing down (in +) Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 16 / 30

title: Read the slope, not the height
text: 2026-XJ · What Changes · Graphic novel, page 26 Read the slope, not the height Supplied practice data on a velocity–time graph rise from zero meters per second at zero seconds to twelve meters per second at four seconds. The slope is positive three meters per second squared. The graph’s height gives velocity. Its slope gives acceleration. These are supplied practice data. What changes if the line is flat at +5 m/s instead? Part 2 · Check the graph and prediction · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 7

title: Equations of motion
text: Reference · constant acceleration ≈ 20 min Equations of motion Velocity v = v₀ + at Position x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² Use these as a reference — no derivation today. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 18 / 30

title: Braking is acceleration too
text: Try it as a group Target R4 Braking is acceleration too A cart moves right at 6 m/s, then right at 2 m/s. Did its velocity change? Is it speeding up or slowing down? Solve alone · compare as a group · then check. Velocity over time The velocity stays positive but gets smaller. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 19 / 30

title: Direction matters
text: See another kind of change Target R4 Direction matters A car turning at a steady speed still changes velocity. The direction changes, even if the speed does not. Same size, new direction Velocity includes direction. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 20 / 30

title: Keep the initial velocity
text: 2026-XJ · What Changes · Graphic novel, page 27 Keep the initial velocity Eli presents a practice cart with initial velocity two meters per second, acceleration three meters per second squared and time four seconds. Nadia calculates final velocity as two plus three times four, which equals fourteen meters per second. The cart already moves at the start. Under constant acceleration, v = v₀ + at. Why does at give the velocity change, rather than always giving the final velocity? Part 2 · Check the graph and prediction · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 7

title: Earth’s pull at the starting separation
text: Back to 2026-XJ ≈ 13 min How much does Earth pull on it right now? Distance r = 1.2 × 10⁸ km = 1.2 × 10¹¹ m Earth's pull a = GM ÷ r² Result a ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ m/s² Earth-only estimate at this separation. It does not include the Sun or prove a long-term forecast accurate. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 22 / 30

title: Gravity changes along the path
text: Looking ahead ≈ 13 min As 2026-XJ gets closer, gravity gets stronger. Constant velocity is a classroom approximation. Gravity changes along the path; Unit 2 improves the model. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 23 / 30

title: A small change is still a change
text: 2026-XJ · What Changes · Graphic novel, page 28 A small change is still a change An Earth-only classroom estimate gives acceleration magnitude 2.8 times ten to the minus eight meters per second squared. If constant for 1.6 times ten to the seven seconds, the change is about 0.448 meters per second. Mr. Antocci says the Sun’s effect is larger here and gravity changes along the path. This is a conditional estimate for a fictional scenario. It is not a complete orbit forecast. Which assumptions must you check before extending this estimate across a long interval? Part 3 · Challenge the model claim · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 7

title: Negative does not mean slow
text: Check a common mix-up Target R4 Negative does not mean slow Negative velocity means motion in the chosen negative direction. Speeding up or slowing down depends on whether velocity and acceleration point the same way. Velocity over time Here speed drops from 6 to 2 m/s, while acceleration is positive. Day 7 · Acceleration Antocci Physics · 27 / 30
